transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well… I guess it’s this scar on my wrist. I know, logically, it’s probably not nearly as noticeable as it feels to me, but when I’m at church or playing bridge, I just get this feeling that everyone’s looking right at it. Like it’s the first thing they see now instead of me. 

And I know people are usually wrapped up in their own things—goodness, at bridge they’re mostly watching the cards anyway—but I still can’t seem to stop thinking about it.
Do you find yourself often worrying about the way you look, not just the scar, but other things too?

Mostly it’s the scar, honestly. I mean, I’ve never been one to fuss too much—well, I suppose everyone has their little things, don’t they? My sister used to spend ages on her hair before church, and I always thought, “Good heavens, we’re only going down the road.”

But with this wrist… I know in my head it’s probably not as bad as it looks to me. Still, when I’m sitting at church or playing bridge, I keep feeling like everyone’s eyes go right to it, like it’s the first thing they notice about me now.
Do you ever find yourself avoiding certain activities or places, like church or bridge club, because you’re worried about people noticing the scar?

Yes… I suppose I have, though I hate admitting that. I haven’t stopped going entirely, but I’ve skipped a few choir things and some theater volunteer commitments because I get so caught up trying to make sure my wrist is covered or won’t draw attention.

And then it sort of spills over—like with my bookkeeping work, I’ve been late turning things in, which isn’t like me. I’ll mean to sit down and finish, and instead I’m fiddling with sleeves or worrying about whether someone noticed it earlier. It sounds silly when I say it out loud, but it does get in the way.
Does the worry about your wrist ever get so bad that it really interferes with your life, like making it hard to focus on anything else or enjoy the things you used to?

Yes… yes, it does, more than I’d like to admit. I’ll sit down to do my bookkeeping, and I’ve always been very careful with numbers—my old supervisor used to say I had an eye like a hawk for a misplaced decimal—but lately I’ll lose time fussing with my sleeve or thinking about whether my wrist showed when I handed someone a paper.

And I’ve been late turning in some work, which is embarrassing. I’ve also skipped a few choir things and theater volunteer commitments because I just get so caught up in making sure it won’t be noticed. I tell myself it’s not a big thing, but then there I am, not going.
Would you say that your concern about the scar on your wrist feels more like worrying about how you look, like a flaw that others might notice, rather than just a reminder of what caused it?

Yes… I think that’s right. I mean, it’s the way it looks that gets to me. I know, in a sensible part of my mind, that the scar probably isn’t nearly as noticeable as it seems to me.

But when I’m at church, or sitting at bridge, I get this feeling that people’s eyes go straight to my wrist. Like before they hear anything I’m saying, they’ve already noticed that. Which is silly, maybe—people have their own worries, don’t they? I remember my mother used to say nobody is looking at you as much as you think they are. But still, with this, it feels like it’s the first thing they see about me now.
